set.seed(735794)
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(rsample)   # group_vfold_cv(), rolling_origin()
library(mgcv)      # gam()
library(genlasso)  # fusedlasso1d()
library(glmnet)
library(grpreg)     # group lasso
library(nhanesA)    # NHANES data pull
library(BGLR)       # wheat data
library(kableExtra)

select <- dplyr::select

1 Scenario 1: NHANES

Goal: Predict systolic blood pressure from demographic and body-measurement variables using a recent NHANES cycle.

Intended CV issue: NHANES uses a complex, clustered survey design. Participants are sampled within primary sampling units (SDMVPSU), nested within strata (SDMVSTRA). Observations within the same PSU are more similar to each other than to observations in a different PSU (shared geography, recruitment site, local population characteristics). A random row-level CV split puts people from the same PSU in both training and validation folds, which overstates performance — the same leakage mechanism as splitting repeated visits on the same subject, just from geographic clustering instead of time.

Intended method: GAM, since age and BMI effects on blood pressure are plausibly nonlinear (we just covered s() terms) and NHANES is large enough to estimate smooth terms comfortably.

1.1 Pulling the Data

demo <- nhanes("DEMO_J")   # 2017-2018 cycle: demographics, SDMVPSU, SDMVSTRA
bpx  <- nhanes("BPX_J")    # blood pressure exam
bmx  <- nhanes("BMX_J")    # body measures

str(demo[, c("SEQN", "RIDAGEYR", "RIAGENDR", "SDMVPSU", "SDMVSTRA")])
'data.frame':   9254 obs. of  5 variables:
 $ SEQN    : num  93703 93704 93705 93706 93707 ...
 $ RIDAGEYR: num  2 2 66 18 13 66 75 0 56 18 ...
 $ RIAGENDR: Factor w/ 2 levels "Male","Female": 2 1 2 1 1 2 2 2 1 1 ...
 $ SDMVPSU : num  2 1 2 2 1 2 1 1 2 2 ...
 $ SDMVSTRA: num  145 143 145 134 138 138 136 134 134 147 ...
# SDMVPSU only takes values 1–2 and is nested within each stratum, 
# not a standalone cluster ID. To get a cluster ID we need to combine
# psu and strata.
nhanes_df <- demo |>
  select(SEQN, age = RIDAGEYR, sex = RIAGENDR, race.eth = RIDRETH3, 
         educ = DMDEDUC2, married = DMDHRMAZ, 
         psu = SDMVPSU, strata = SDMVSTRA) |>
  left_join(bpx |> select(SEQN, sysBP = BPXSY1), by = "SEQN") |>
  left_join(bmx |> select(SEQN, BMI = BMXBMI), by = "SEQN")  |> 
  mutate(cluster = interaction(strata, psu, drop = TRUE)) |>
  drop_na()

1.2 The Wrong Way: Naive Row-Level CV

set.seed(1)
folds_naive <- vfold_cv(nhanes_df, v = 5)

rmse_naive <- map_dbl(folds_naive$splits, function(s) {
  tr <- analysis(s); va <- assessment(s)
  fit <- gam(sysBP ~ s(age, by = sex) + s(BMI, by = sex) + sex + 
               race.eth + educ + married, data = tr, method = "REML")
  sqrt(mean((va$sysBP - predict(fit, newdata = va))^2))
})

mean(rmse_naive)
[1] 16.55477

1.3 The Right Way: Grouping by Cluster

set.seed(1)
folds_psu <- group_vfold_cv(nhanes_df, group = cluster, v = 5)

rmse_grouped <- map_dbl(folds_psu$splits, function(s) {
  tr <- analysis(s); va <- assessment(s)
  fit <- gam(sysBP ~ s(age, by = sex) + s(BMI, by = sex) + sex + 
               race.eth + educ + married, data = tr, method = "REML")
  sqrt(mean((va$sysBP - predict(fit, newdata = va))^2))
})

mean(rmse_grouped)
[1] 16.55789
tibble(
  CV_design = c("Naive (row-level)", "Grouped by Cluster"),
  Mean_RMSE = c(mean(rmse_naive), mean(rmse_grouped))
)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  CV_design          Mean_RMSE
  <chr>                  <dbl>
1 Naive (row-level)       16.6
2 Grouped by Cluster      16.6

Debrief point: if the naive CV RMSE is meaningfully lower than the grouped CV RMSE, that gap is the leakage — it’s an estimate of how much the model was “cheating” by seeing correlated observations from the same PSU on both sides of the split.

1.4 A New Question: Does Error Vary by Race/Ethnicity

In this particular dataset, the overall naive vs. grouped RMSE comparison earlier didn’t show much of a gap — so it might be tempting to assume the subgroup breakdown above is fine as is. However, a small or absent gap in the overall RMSE doesn’t guarantee a small gap in every subgroup’s RMSE, since leakage severity can vary by how concentrated each group is across PSUs. The only way to know is to rerun the breakdown on folds_psu and compare directly, I’ve done that and there still isn’t a difference. However, here, we’ll still use the correct folds_psu.

set.seed(1)
grouped_preds <- map_dfr(folds_psu$splits, function(s) {
  tr <- analysis(s); va <- assessment(s)
  fit <- gam(sysBP ~ s(age, by = sex) + s(BMI, by = sex) + sex +
               race.eth + educ + married, data = tr, method = "REML")

  va |>
    mutate(pred = predict(fit, newdata = va)) |>
    select(race.eth, sysBP, pred)
})

rmse_by_race_grouped <- grouped_preds |>
  mutate(sq_err = (sysBP - pred)^2) |>
  group_by(race.eth) |>
  summarize(
    n       = n(),
    avg_obs = mean(sysBP),
    avg_pred = mean(pred),
    mse     = mean(sq_err),
    se_mse  = sd(sq_err) / sqrt(n),
    rmse    = sqrt(mse),
    se_rmse = se_mse / (2 * rmse),        # delta method: SE(sqrt(x)) ~= SE(x) / (2*sqrt(x))
    ci_lower = rmse - 1.96 * se_rmse,
    ci_upper = rmse + 1.96 * se_rmse,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(rmse))

rmse_by_race_grouped |>
  transmute(
    `Race/Ethnicity` = race.eth,
    `n`              = n,
    `Avg Obs` = round(avg_obs,1),
    `Avg Pred` = round(avg_pred,1),
    `Avg Diff` = round(avg_obs - avg_pred,2),
    `RMSE`           = round(rmse, 2),
    `SE`             = round(se_rmse, 3),
    `95% CI`         = paste0("(", round(ci_lower, 2), ", ", round(ci_upper, 2), ")")
  ) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrr", caption = "RMSE by Race/Ethnicity with Approximate 95% CIs")

2 Scenario 2: Testing Volume and Percent Positive

Goal: Using weekly test-volume and percent-positive data from the five most populous states, predict (a) total weekly specimens tested and (b) percent positive, for future weeks.

CV issue: Two, layered. First, temporal ordering — the outcome in week \(t\) is correlated with weeks \(t-1, t-2, \dots\), so a random split lets the model see the future. CV has to be a rolling-origin / forward-chaining design. Second, if state is entered as a fixed effect, the fitted model cannot generalize to a state it never saw in training — worth surfacing even though we aren’t holding out a state here, because it constrains what this model can and can’t be used for later.

Intended methods: GAM and fused lasso (captures the piecewise trend / regime shifts in each state’s series — a direct callback to the fused-lasso lesson). For state we can use a fixed-effects linear model since there are only 5 states.

2.1 Data Setup

This uses CDC’s ILINet clinical-lab surveillance file directly. I downloaded this from the web.

flu_raw <- read_csv("ICL_NREVSS_Clinical_Labs.csv", skip = 1, na = "X") |>
  clean_names()

top5_states <- c("California", "Texas", "Florida", "New York", "Pennsylvania")

flu_df <- flu_raw |>
  rename(state = region,
         total_tests  = total_specimens,
         pct_positive = percent_positive) |>
  filter(state %in% top5_states) |>
  arrange(state, year, week) |>          # chronological order WITHIN each state
  select(state, year, week, total_tests, pct_positive) |>
  group_by(state) |>
  mutate(t = row_number()) |>            # sequential time index that respects year + week
  ungroup() 

flu_df |> count(state)
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  state            n
  <chr>        <int>
1 California     569
2 Florida        569
3 New York       569
4 Pennsylvania   569
5 Texas          569
Note

If I was modeling this data, I would log-transform the pct_positive variable. Here, for clean interpretations, we won’t do this.

Important

week alone resets every season (1–52/53), so ordering by week without year first silently interleaves different flu seasons — week 40 of 2015 would sort next to week 40 of 2019. arrange(state, year, week) fixes the chronology; t is then a clean sequential index per state that both the rolling-origin split and the fused lasso can rely on.

2.2 Why the Two “Obvious” Approaches Don’t Actually Answer the Question

The handout goal is genuine forecasting — total specimens and percent positive for a future week/year, e.g., California, 2026, week 50. That requirement rules out a couple of approaches:

  • Fused lasso on the raw time series estimates one coefficient per observed time point. There is no coefficient for “week 50 of 2026” because that row doesn’t exist in the fitted path — the model has nothing to extrapolate with. It’s a good descriptive tool for finding past regime shifts, but not a predictive one for a genuinely new time point.
  • week_num as a sequential index fed into a fixed-effects model has the same problem in a different place: it’s tied to the training data’s specific rows, not a reusable calendar concept. There’s no principled way to hand the model “week_num = (whatever a 2026 week-50 row would have been).”

What actually generalizes to a new year/week is a model with separate, interpretable terms for week and year: a cyclic seasonal effect for week (defined for all 52 weeks, so no extrapolation needed there at all) and a linear trend for year (which can be extrapolated, honestly, a few years out). state re-enters as a plain fixed effect — a factor term.

2.3 Model: GAM with Cyclic Week Smooth + Linear Year + State Fixed Effect

gam_fit <- gam(
  pct_positive ~ state + s(week, bs = "cc", k = 10) + year,
  data   = flu_df,
  knots  = list(week = c(0.5, 52.5)),   # ties week 52 back to week 1
  method = "REML"
)

plot(gam_fit, select = 1, shade = TRUE, main = "Seasonal effect of week (cyclic)")

s(week, bs = "cc") is a cyclic cubic smooth — it forces the fitted curve at week 52 to connect back to week 1, the right assumption for a seasonal effect (there’s no real discontinuity between the last week of one flu season and the first week of the next). year enters linearly, so it contributes a single extrapolable slope rather than a value tied to specific observed years. state is a plain factor term — a fixed effect exactly as requested, fit directly in gam().

Note

refund::pfr() would fit this identical model — it’s built directly on top of mgcv::gam() and accepts the same formula syntax when there’s no functional predictor involved. gam() is used here because nothing in this formula is actually functional (unlike the DTI example); pfr() becomes necessary once you have a genuine curve as a predictor, not before.

2.4 Honest Error Estimation: Rolling-Origin CV, Actually Used

The roll object above illustrated the idea of rolling-origin splits on a single state. The number we actually need — the expected forecast error of the model above — requires applying that same logic to the full pooled panel, refitting at each cutoff and scoring on the weeks immediately after.

flu_df <- flu_df |>
  mutate(calendar_t = (year - min(year)) * 52 + week) |>
  arrange(calendar_t, state)

weeks_sorted  <- sort(unique(flu_df$calendar_t))
initial_weeks <- 104   # ~2 seasons before the first forecast
horizon_weeks <- 4     # forecast 4 weeks ahead at each cutoff

cutoffs <- weeks_sorted[initial_weeks:(length(weeks_sorted) - horizon_weeks)]
cutoffs[1:5]
[1] 143 144 145 146 147
cv_results <- map_dfr(cutoffs, function(cut) {
  train <- flu_df |> filter(calendar_t <= cut)
  test  <- flu_df |> filter(calendar_t > cut, calendar_t <= cut + horizon_weeks)
  if (nrow(test) == 0) return(NULL)

  fit <- gam(pct_positive ~ state + s(week, bs = "cc", k = 10) + year,
             data = train, knots = list(week = c(0.5, 52.5)), method = "REML")

  tibble(
    cutoff = cut,
    rmse   = sqrt(mean((test$pct_positive - predict(fit, newdata = test))^2, na.rm = TRUE))
  )
})

head(cv_results)
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  cutoff  rmse
   <dbl> <dbl>
1    143  1.40
2    144  1.85
3    145  2.52
4    146  3.21
5    147  4.42
6    148  5.02
mean(cv_results$rmse)
[1] 5.503506
min_year <- min(flu_df$year)

cv_results <- cv_results |>
  mutate(
    approx_year = min_year + (cutoff - 1) %/% 52,
    approx_week = (cutoff - 1) %% 52 + 1,
    # Approximate date for the start of that MMWR week (good enough for plotting)
    approx_date = as.Date(paste0(approx_year, "-01-01")) + (approx_week - 1) * 7
  )

ggplot(cv_results, aes(approx_date, rmse)) +
  # Shade Dec-Feb each year so winter/flu-season is visible at a glance
  annotate("rect",
           xmin = as.Date(paste0(min_year:(min_year + 10), "-12-01"))[-c(1,2)],
           xmax = as.Date(paste0((min_year + 1):(min_year + 11), "-03-01"))[-c(1,2)],
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "Rolling-Origin Forecast Error Over Time",
       x = "Training cutoff (date)", y = "RMSE (4-week-ahead forecast)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

This refits gam() at every cutoff using only data available up to that point, then evaluates on the following month — exactly how the model would be used in practice. mean(cv_results$rmse) is the number to report as the model’s expected forecast error, not any single train/test split.

Important

This loop refits the model dozens of times, which is the honest cost of doing CV properly for a forecasting model. Resist the temptation to shortcut it with a single holdout at the end — one split gives a noisy point estimate, not a distribution you can trust.

2.5 Forecasting a Genuinely Future Observation

final_fit <- gam(pct_positive ~ state + s(week, bs = "cc", k = 10) + year,
                  data = flu_df, knots = list(week = c(0.5, 52.5)), method = "REML")

future_point <- tibble(state = "California", year = 2026, week = 50)
predict(final_fit, newdata = future_point, se.fit = TRUE)
$fit
       1 
8.408783 

$se.fit
        1 
0.4561324
Important

This prediction is only as trustworthy as the linear extrapolation in year. The seasonal week effect is well-supported (fit on the full observed cycle), but the year coefficient is extrapolating past the last observed year and cannot know about a genuine future disruption (a new variant, another pandemic-scale event). Report the rolling-origin CV RMSE alongside any such forecast as the honest uncertainty, and treat a multi-year-out extrapolation as considerably shakier than a same-season forecast.

The same approach — cyclic week smooth, linear year, state fixed effect, rolling-origin CV — applies to total_tests: refit with total_tests ~ state + s(week, bs = "cc", k = 10) + year and repeat the CV loop above.

Important

The limitation to flag explicitly. A fixed effect for state is estimated only for the states in the training data. There is no mechanism in this model for predicting a sixth state that wasn’t part of the fit — the model has literally no parameter for it. If the eventual goal is a model that generalizes to new states (not just the five here), a fixed-effects approach is the wrong tool; you’d want something that treats state as a random effect or borrows strength across states (e.g., a hierarchical model), which is beyond what we’ve covered so far. Worth having the group articulate this limitation even though it doesn’t change what they fit today.

2.5.1 Repeating for log-transformed outcome

Below, I’m repeating the entire thing for a log transformed outcome:

flu_df <- flu_df |>
  mutate(l_pct_positive = log(if_else(pct_positive==0, 1/total_tests*100, pct_positive))) |>
  arrange(calendar_t, state)

weeks_sorted  <- sort(unique(flu_df$calendar_t))
initial_weeks <- 104   # ~2 seasons before the first forecast
horizon_weeks <- 4     # forecast 4 weeks ahead at each cutoff

cutoffs <- weeks_sorted[initial_weeks:(length(weeks_sorted) - horizon_weeks)]

cv_results <- map_dfr(cutoffs, function(cut) {
  train <- flu_df |> filter(calendar_t <= cut)
  test  <- flu_df |> filter(calendar_t > cut, calendar_t <= cut + horizon_weeks)
  if (nrow(test) == 0) return(NULL)

  fit <- gam(l_pct_positive ~ state + s(week, bs = "cc", k = 10) + year,
             data = train, knots = list(week = c(0.5, 52.5)), method = "REML")

  tibble(
    cutoff = cut,
    rmse   = sqrt(mean((test$pct_positive - predict(fit, newdata = test))^2, na.rm = TRUE))
  )
})

mean(cv_results$rmse)
[1] 6.454972
min_year <- min(flu_df$year)

cv_results <- cv_results |>
  mutate(
    approx_year = min_year + (cutoff - 1) %/% 52,
    approx_week = (cutoff - 1) %% 52 + 1,
    # Approximate date for the start of that MMWR week (good enough for plotting)
    approx_date = as.Date(paste0(approx_year, "-01-01")) + (approx_week - 1) * 7
  )

ggplot(cv_results, aes(approx_date, rmse)) +
  # Shade Dec-Feb each year so winter/flu-season is visible at a glance
  annotate("rect",
           xmin = as.Date(paste0(min_year:(min_year + 10), "-12-01"))[-c(1,2)],
           xmax = as.Date(paste0((min_year + 1):(min_year + 11), "-03-01"))[-c(1,2)],
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "Rolling-Origin Forecast Error Over Time",
       x = "Training cutoff (date)", y = "RMSE (4-week-ahead forecast)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
final_fit <- gam(l_pct_positive ~ state + s(week, bs = "cc", k = 10) + year,
                  data = flu_df, knots = list(week = c(0.5, 52.5)), method = "REML")

future_point <- tibble(state = "California", year = 2026, week = 50)
pred_vals <- predict(final_fit, newdata = future_point, se.fit = TRUE)

tibble(pred = exp(pred_vals$fit), se.fit = pred_vals$se.fit*exp(pred_vals$fit))

2.6 Fused Lasso

For fun, I wanted to fit this model with the fused LASSO. What’s cool about this is that I can fuse the coefficients in two directions year and week. Let’s check it out:

# ============================================================
# Step 1: Fit the 2D fused lasso on years up to 2024 (holding out 2025)
# ============================================================
fused_train <- flu_df |>
  filter(state == "California") |>
  filter(year > 2015 & year < 2025 & week < 53) |>   # complete years, 2025 excluded
  arrange(year, week)                                 # week must vary fastest within each year

dim1 <- length(unique(fused_train$week))   # 52 weeks
dim2 <- length(unique(fused_train$year))   # years 2016-2024

fl_train <- fusedlasso2d(fused_train$pct_positive, dim1 = dim1, dim2 = dim2)

# Grab a fine path of lambdas so the validation curve below isn't lumpy
a_train <- coef(fl_train, nlam = 30)

# ============================================================
# Keep the 3x3 plot of coefficients from the TRAINING-ONLY fit
# (same 9-lambda snapshot as before, just refit without 2025)
# ============================================================
a9 <- coef(fl_train, nlam = 9)

par(mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1), mfrow = c(3, 3))
cols <- rainbow(100)
zlim <- range(a9$beta)
for (i in 1:9) {
  image(matrix(a9$beta[, i], nrow = dim1), col = cols, zlim = zlim, axes = FALSE)
  mtext(bquote(lambda == .(sprintf("%.3f", a9$lambda[i]))))
}
# ============================================================
# Step 2: Predict 2025 from the training fit, at every lambda,
# and see which lambda gives the lowest holdout error
# ============================================================

# The fused lasso has no coefficient beyond the training grid, so the natural
# forecast for a year it never saw is the LAST fitted year's curve
# (total-variation regularization assumes adjacent cells are similar --
# "next year looks like last year" is the model's own implied forecast).

weeks_grid <- sort(unique(fused_train$week))

holdout_2025 <- flu_df |>
  filter(state == "California", year == 2025, week < 53) |>
  arrange(week)

forecast_rmse <- map_dbl(seq_along(a_train$lambda), function(j) {
  beta_mat <- matrix(a_train$beta[, j], nrow = dim1, ncol = dim2)
  last_year_col <- beta_mat[, dim2]                # fitted 2024 curve
  names(last_year_col) <- weeks_grid

  pred_2025 <- last_year_col[as.character(holdout_2025$week)]
  sqrt(mean((holdout_2025$pct_positive - pred_2025)^2, na.rm = TRUE))
})

lambda_err <- tibble(lambda = a_train$lambda, rmse = forecast_rmse)

ggplot(lambda_err, aes(lambda, rmse)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "Validation Error by Lambda (2025 Held Out)",
       x = expression(lambda ~ "(log scale)"),
       y = "RMSE, 2025 forecast vs. actual (log percent positive)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
lambda_best <- lambda_err$lambda[which.min(lambda_err$rmse)]
lambda_best
[1] 33.93791
# ============================================================
# Step 3: Refit at lambda_best using ALL data (now including 2025),
# display the coefficients with ggplot
# ============================================================
fused_full <- flu_df |>
  filter(state == "California") |>
  filter(year > 2015 & year < 2026 & week < 53) |>
  arrange(year, week)

dim1_full <- length(unique(fused_full$week))
dim2_full <- length(unique(fused_full$year))

fl_full <- fusedlasso2d(fused_full$pct_positive, dim1 = dim1_full, dim2 = dim2_full)

beta_full <- coef(fl_full, lambda = lambda_best)$beta

plot_full <- fused_full |>
  mutate(Beta = as.vector(beta_full),
         year_f = factor(year))

ggplot(plot_full, aes(week, Beta, color = year_f)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = paste0("2D Fused Lasso Coefficients, Full Data (\u03bb = ",
                       round(lambda_best, 3), ")"),
       x = "Week", y = "Beta", color = "Year") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
# ============================================================
# Step 4: Predict 2025 week 50 from the full refit, then carry that
# forward as the prediction for 2026 week 50
# ============================================================
weeks_grid_full <- sort(unique(fused_full$week))
years_grid_full  <- sort(unique(fused_full$year))

beta_mat_full <- matrix(beta_full, nrow = dim1_full, ncol = dim2_full,
                         dimnames = list(weeks_grid_full, years_grid_full))

pred_2025_wk50 <- beta_mat_full[as.character(50), as.character(2025)]
pred_2026_wk50 <- pred_2025_wk50   # no coefficient exists beyond the observed grid

tibble(
  year = c(2025, 2026),
  week = 50,
  predicted_pct_positive = c(pred_2025_wk50, pred_2026_wk50))
# A tibble: 2 × 3
   year  week predicted_pct_positive
  <dbl> <dbl>                  <dbl>
1  2025    50                   6.09
2  2026    50                   6.09
Important

Notice the 2026 prediction is identical to the 2025 one — the fused lasso literally has no parameter for a cell outside the fitted grid, so “predicting 2026” here just means assuming next year looks like the last observed year. That’s a fine baseline, but it’s a much weaker extrapolation than the year-as-linear-term GAM from earlier in this document, which can actually project a trend forward. Worth having students compare the two 2026 forecasts side by side.

3 Scenario 3: BGLR Wheat

Goal: Using genetic marker data on a panel of wheat lines, predict yield in a new growing environment using a model trained on other environments.

Intended CV issue: This is a target-context mismatch, not a random-split problem. The same lines are phenotyped in multiple environments, and the genetic effect on yield can differ by environment (G×E interaction) — a model fit on environments 1–3 may not transfer cleanly to environment 4, which is structurally the same issue as a model failing to generalize across populations, sites, or cohorts. The honest evaluation is to hold out an entire environment, never a random subset of line-by-environment combinations.

Intended method: Lasso, this will provide variable selection and prediction of new values.

3.1 Data

data(wheat)
str(wheat.X[, 1:5])
 num [1:599, 1:5] 0 1 1 0 0 1 1 1 0 0 ...
 - attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2
  ..$ : NULL
  ..$ : chr [1:5] "wPt.0538" "wPt.8463" "wPt.6348" "wPt.9992" ...
str(wheat.Y)
 num [1:599, 1:4] 1.672 -0.253 0.342 0.785 0.998 ...
 - attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2
  ..$ : chr [1:599] "775" "2166" "2167" "2465" ...
  ..$ : chr [1:4] "1" "2" "4" "5"
X <- wheat.X
Y <- wheat.Y
colnames(Y)
[1] "1" "2" "4" "5"
Note

wheat.Y has one column per environment. The code below assumes the first column is the held-out one and the last three are the training environments.

3.2 Held-Out Environment Design

train_envs <- 2:4
test_env   <- 1

y_train <- rowMeans(Y[, train_envs], na.rm = TRUE)  # average across training environments
y_test  <- Y[, test_env]

keep <- complete.cases(X) & !is.na(y_train) & !is.na(y_test)
X_fit  <- X[keep, ]
y_fit  <- y_train[keep]
y_eval <- y_test[keep]

3.3 Lasso

cv_fit <- cv.glmnet(X_fit, y_fit, nfolds = 10, alpha = 1)
plot(cv_fit)
lambda_best <- cv_fit$lambda.min
lambda_1se <- cv_fit$lambda.1se

lasso_min  <- glmnet(X_fit, y_fit, alpha = 1, lambda = lambda_best,  standardize = TRUE)
lasso_1se  <- glmnet(X_fit, y_fit, alpha = 1, lambda = lambda_1se,  standardize = TRUE)

3.4 Evaluating Transfer to the Held-Out Environment

pred_test <- predict(lasso_min, X_fit)
pred_test_1se <- predict(lasso_1se, X_fit)

tibble(
  metric = c("RMSE", "Correlation", "Non-zero Coeffs"),
  Best  = c(
    sqrt(mean((y_eval - pred_test)^2)),
    cor(y_eval, pred_test), 
    sum(coef(lasso_min )[-1]!=0)
  ),
  One_SE  = c(
    sqrt(mean((y_eval - pred_test_1se)^2)),
    cor(y_eval, pred_test_1se), 
    sum(coef(lasso_1se )[-1]!=0)
  )
)
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  metric             Best  One_SE
  <chr>             <dbl>   <dbl>
1 RMSE              1.12   1.07  
2 Correlation      -0.114 -0.0798
3 Non-zero Coeffs 101     55     
tibble(observed = y_eval, predicted = as.numeric(pred_test)) |>
  ggplot(aes(observed, predicted)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Held-Out Environment: Observed vs. Predicted",
       x = "Observed yield (env 4)", y = "Predicted yield (trained on envs 1-3)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

3.5 Naive Comparison: Ordinary CV Ignoring Environment

Rather than holding out an entire environment, we could instead pool every line-by-environment observation into one long dataset and run standard random k-fold CV on it — treating each row as if it were independent. This is the version many people reach for by default; here’s why it’s misleading for this data.

# Stack ALL environments (not just the training ones) into a long dataset:
# one row per line-by-environment combination. Random folds below don't
# know that the same genetic line shows up once per environment.

env_cols <- colnames(Y)[1:4]

y_long  <- as.vector(Y[, env_cols])
X_long  <- X[rep(seq_len(nrow(X)), times = length(env_cols)), ]
line_id <- rep(seq_len(nrow(X)), times = length(env_cols))

keep_long <- complete.cases(X_long) & !is.na(y_long)
X_long_fit  <- X_long[keep_long, ]
y_long_fit  <- y_long[keep_long]
line_long_fit <- line_id[keep_long]

nrow(X_long_fit)
[1] 2396
set.seed(1)
cv_naive <- cv.glmnet(X_long_fit, y_long_fit, nfolds = 10, alpha = 1)
plot(cv_naive)
# cv.glmnet's cvm at the chosen lambda is mean CV squared error
# for a gaussian family, so sqrt(cvm) is directly comparable to the
# RMSE reported for the honest environment-transfer evaluation above.
rmse_naive_cv <- sqrt(min(cv_naive$cvm))
rmse_naive_cv
[1] 0.9456668
tibble(
  Design = c("Naive CV (pooled, random folds, ignores environment)",
             "Honest environment transfer (train envs 1-3, test env 4)"),
  RMSE = c(rmse_naive_cv, sqrt(mean((y_eval - pred_test)^2)))
)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Design                                                    RMSE
  <chr>                                                    <dbl>
1 Naive CV (pooled, random folds, ignores environment)     0.946
2 Honest environment transfer (train envs 1-3, test env 4) 1.12 
# Percent difference
round((rmse_naive_cv- sqrt(mean((y_eval - pred_test)^2)))/rmse_naive_cv,3)*100
[1] -18.7
Important

Why the naive number looks better. Each line appears once per environment, so it contributes up to four rows to X_long_fit — one per environment — all sharing the same genotype. Random folds don’t keep a line’s rows together, so a line’s environment-4 phenotype can end up in the validation fold while that same line’s environment-1/2/3 phenotypes (and identical X row) sit in the training fold. The model can partly recognize the line from its genotype and lean on what it already “knows” about that line’s phenotype in other environments, rather than learning a genotype effect that genuinely transfers to a new environment. The gap between these two RMSEs is an estimate of exactly that — the same leakage mechanism flagged for NHANES, just clustered by genetic line instead of by PSU.
